analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage to $6.50 an hour and denies tax deductions for executive pay more than 25 times the lowest salary.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour [S2][S3]. It would also change the tax code so employers could no longer deduct executive pay that exceeds 25 times what their lowest-paid employee makes [S2][S3]. A worker making the minimum wage would get a raise of about $4,700 a year working full time; corporations paying huge salaries would pay more in taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid less than $6.50 an hour would get an immediate raise once the bill took effect — a jump of more than 50% from the $4.25 floor in place at the time [S3]. The Tax Policy Center-style effect runs the other way too: companies that pay some employees more than 25 times their lowest wage would owe more taxes, since they could no longer deduct that pay as a business expense [S3]. Everyone earning near the minimum would see the biggest gains.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour, effective 90 days after enactment — an increase of more than 50% for workers at the bottom [S2][S3].

Denies employers a business-expense tax deduction for any employee's salary, wages, or bonuses above 25 times the compensation of the company's lowest-paid employee, a rule aimed at the widening gap between top and bottom pay [S2][S3].

Applies the pay-ratio rule across the whole corporate group — related companies treated as a single employer count together, so firms could not dodge it by assigning low-paid staff to a subsidiary [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with many minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, and other low-wage industries — would bear higher payroll costs [S3]. Corporations paying executives more than 25 times their lowest wage would lose a tax deduction and owe more federal tax [S2][S3]. Some of those costs could show up in prices or fewer low-wage jobs, the standard objection to a large minimum-wage increase.

drawbacks.text: A more-than-50% jump in the wage floor over just 90 days is far larger than past increases; low-wage employers argue steep hikes can push some businesses to cut hours, raise prices, or shed entry-level jobs, and small businesses would have the least time to adjust [S3].

The executive-pay rule is easy to sidestep: it covers only salary, wages, and bonuses, so companies could shift top pay into stock options, perks, or deferred compensation that the definition does not touch, while still facing higher taxes on covered pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The raise for low-wage workers would be large and immediate, and the tax change is a narrow, targeted way to discourage extreme pay gaps rather than a broad tax hike. The main honest objections are the speed of the increase — 90 days leaves little room for small employers — and the weakness of the pay-ratio rule, which motivated companies could route around through equity pay. On balance the bill would transfer money from profitable firms and their top earners to the lowest-paid workers, but its design is rough in places.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and neither ever brought it up — it simply died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Sabo introduced the bill on January 20, 1995, and it was referred to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities and to the Ways and Means Committee [S3][S5].
Thirty members cosponsored it: 28 Democrats and 2 Independents; no Republicans signed on [S4].
On February 1, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and that is where it stayed [S5].

The only further action was a second round of introductory remarks by the sponsor in March 1996; no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of low-wage workers kept the $4.25 minimum for another year and a half, and large companies kept deducting executive pay from their taxes. A smaller minimum-wage increase to $5.15 was enacted later in 1996 through separate legislation, but the $6.50 proposal and the pay-ratio rule never came to a vote.

for.name: Rep. Martin Olav Sabo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor twice, in January 1995 and March 1996

against.name: Rep. William Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Chaired the primary committee the bill was referred to; the bill went to a subcommittee and was never scheduled for a markup or vote

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee with jurisdiction over the tax provision; the bill was never taken up there

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents, with no Republican support listed, and the Republican-majority committees never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, and other large users of minimum-wage labor)
industries.note: The bill would raise their wage floor from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour, raising payroll costs by more than half for their lowest-paid staff [S3]. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the wage gains workers would have received.

industries.industry: Large corporations paying top executives over 25 times their lowest wage
industries.note: They would lose a business tax deduction for the portion of executive salary, wages, and bonuses above 25 times the lowest-paid employee, increasing their federal tax bill [S2][S3].
